body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Direct cessation versus stepwise weaning of high-flow nasal cannula in infants with bronchiolitis: a randomised trial","authors":"Okonjo-Reyes A, Lindqvist-Barros M, Tamura-Holt E","year":2022,"venue":"Pediatric Respiratory Research","doi":"10.5555/prr.2022.0317","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We randomly allocated 184 infants aged 1 to 24 months with bronchiolitis on high-flow nasal cannula to direct cessation once stable for two hours in FiO2 of 40 percent or less, or to stepwise weaning of flow. Time on high flow was shorter with direct cessation (median 26 against 44 hours), and length of stay fell by a median of 18 hours. Re-escalation to high flow within 24 hours occurred in 11 percent with direct cessation and 8 percent with stepwise weaning, a difference compatible with chance. Infants younger than 3 months made up 21 percent of participants. No infant required intubation."},{"title":"Re-escalation after abrupt discontinuation of high-flow support in young infants: a multicentre observational study","authors":"Varela-Nkosi T, Brandstrom-Ade O","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Pediatric Hospital Care","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across five pediatric wards, we compared 1,030 infants with bronchiolitis whose high flow was stopped abruptly with those weaned stepwise, according to local practice. Among infants younger than 8 weeks, re-escalation within 48 hours occurred in 24 percent after abrupt discontinuation and 12 percent after stepwise weaning (adjusted odds ratio 2.1). In older infants there was no difference. PICU transfer was rare in both groups. Wards that used abrupt discontinuation also admitted younger and sicker infants, and residual confounding is likely."},{"title":"A ward-based weaning protocol for high-flow nasal cannula in bronchiolitis: a quality improvement report","authors":"Fitzsimmons-Obi K, Arakawa-Lund P, Mensah-Carlyle J","year":2021,"venue":"Hospital Quality and Safety in Children","doi":"10.5555/hqsc.2021.0145","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We introduced a nurse-driven weaning protocol for high-flow nasal cannula on a general pediatric ward over three PDSA cycles in one winter. Median time on high flow fell from 49 to 30 hours on the run chart, with a shift sustained for 11 weeks. Length of stay fell from 3.4 to 2.7 days. Readmission within 7 days was unchanged at 3 percent, and PICU transfers fell slightly. Protocol adherence at night was 62 percent compared with 85 percent during the day, and most missed trials off occurred after midnight."},{"title":"Stepwise weaning is not needed after high-flow therapy in bronchiolitis: an individual patient analysis from three hospitals","authors":"Delgado-Imani S, Wren-Oyelaran B","year":null,"venue":"Pediatric Respiratory Research preprint series","providerType":"preprint","abstract":"Using routinely collected data from three hospitals, we analysed 2,410 episodes of high-flow therapy for bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months, comparing direct cessation with stepwise weaning. After adjustment for age, oxygen requirement and hospital, re-escalation within 24 hours did not differ (8.9 against 9.4 percent), including in infants younger than 8 weeks (13.1 against 12.4 percent). Time on high flow was 20 hours shorter with direct cessation. This preprint has not been peer reviewed, and its listing does not give a year of posting."},{"title":"Parents' experience of high-flow nasal cannula and weaning decisions for infants with bronchiolitis","authors":"Achterberg-Moyo L, Castellano-Reid H","year":2019,"venue":"Family-Centred Nursing","doi":"10.5555/fcn.2019.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held structured conversations with 32 parents of infants treated with high-flow nasal cannula on two pediatric wards. Parents described the high flow as frightening at first and later as a barrier to feeding and holding their baby. Many did not understand why weaning took so long once their baby looked well, and inconsistent explanations from different doctors increased their worry. Parents wanted to be told the criteria for stopping and restarting high flow. Conversations took place on the ward, which may have limited criticism."},{"title":"Two-hourly respiratory assessments at night on pediatric wards: nurse workload during the bronchiolitis season","authors":"Huang-Mbeki R, Soderberg-Nwosu C","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Pediatric Hospital Care","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We timed respiratory assessments on three pediatric wards during a bronchiolitis season. A structured assessment took a median of 6 minutes, and nurses caring for four infants on high flow spent about a quarter of each night hour on assessments. Scheduled assessments were missed in 18 percent of night hours and 6 percent of day hours. Missed assessments were most common between 02:00 and 05:00. Wards with a respiratory therapist overnight missed fewer assessments. The authors suggest weaning protocols set assessment frequencies that night staffing can deliver."},{"title":"Variation in high-flow weaning practice among pediatric hospitalists: a national survey","authors":"Obradovic-Ansah D, Kline-Matsuda F","year":2016,"venue":"Pediatric Hospitalist Perspectives","doi":"10.5555/php.2016.0412","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed 412 pediatric hospitalists about how they wean high-flow nasal cannula in bronchiolitis. Forty-six percent used stepwise flow reduction, 31 percent stopped high flow directly once oxygen requirements were low, and 23 percent varied by patient. Only 18 percent of respondents worked in hospitals with a written weaning protocol. Respondents who feared re-escalation most often cited young infant age and night-time staffing. Most respondents said they would follow a local protocol if one existed. The response rate was 44 percent, and hospitalists in teaching hospitals were over-represented."}]}
